# Assignment

`←` gives a value a name. The target is the run just before `←`, and the value is everything to its right. Besides plain names, a target can be a selection, a dot path, a subscript or a list of names. A function between the target and `←` makes a modified assignment. [Assign](glyphs/assign.qmd) is the reference entry, and [Assignment](rules.qmd#assignment) gives the rule for reading targets.

## Plain assignment

`x←Y` binds `x` to `Y`, which can be an array, a function or an operator. An assignment returns its value without displaying it, so assignments can be chained. Independent assignments need `⋄`, because `a←1 b←2` gives `a` the value of `1 b←2`.

```bpl
x←3 ⋄ x+2          ⍝ 5
sum←+/ ⋄ sum 1 2 3 ⍝ 6
a←b←3 ⋄ a+b        ⍝ 6
```

The name `_` discards a value: `_←Y` evaluates `Y` and keeps nothing.

## Modified assignment

`x f←Y` sets `x` to `x f Y`. A named function goes in parentheses, `x(f)←Y`, because in `x f←Y` the target would be `f`.

```bpl
x←10 ⋄ x+←3 ⋄ x    ⍝ 13
s←"abc" ⋄ s,←"d" ⋄ s ⍝ "abcd"
f←× ⋄ y←3 ⋄ y(f)←4 ⋄ y ⍝ 12
```

## Assigning to part of an array

A target can name part of an array, and the assignment replaces only that part. A [subscript](scripts.qmd#subscripts) writes one literal position. A dot path writes a field, and dot brackets write positions. Other selections go in parentheses, as `(f x)←Y`, where `f` only selects or rearranges, as for structural [Under](glyphs/under.qmd). Each form also works with modified assignment.

```bpl
v←1 2 3 ⋄ v₁←9 ⋄ v           ⍝ 1 9 3
v←1 2 3 ⋄ v.[[0 2]]+←10 ⋄ v  ⍝ 11 2 13
v←1 2 3 ⋄ (2↑v)←8 9 ⋄ v      ⍝ 8 9 3
M←[1 2 ⋄ 3 4] ⋄ ((0⌷⍤1) M)←9 ⋄ M ⍝ [9 2 ⋄ 9 4]
```

A plain assignment to a dot path creates any missing records along the path. A subscript can follow a dot path.

```bpl
T←["n":1]
T.n+←1 ⋄ T.n               ⍝ 2
T.addr.city←"SF" ⋄ T.addr.city ⍝ "SF"
T.a←[1 2] ⋄ T.a₁←7 ⋄ T.a   ⍝ 1 7
```

## Destructuring

A list of names in brackets destructures. Each name gets the matching item, by position. A single value goes to every name, and a nested list of names destructures a nested value. A vector with a key for every item is matched by key instead. Each name gets the item whose key is that name, and items that no name takes are left out. A program takes names from a [module](modules.qmd) this way, as in `[disp]←•load "lib/array.bpl"`. Inside brackets every name is a target, even a name that holds a function.

```bpl
[a b]←10 20 ⋄ a+b          ⍝ 30
[c d]←5 ⋄ c d              ⍝ 5 5
[e [f g]]←1 (2 3) ⋄ g      ⍝ 3
[h i]←1 2 ⋄ [h i]+←10 ⋄ h i ⍝ 11 12
[b a]←["a":1 "b":2 "c":3] ⋄ a b ⍝ 1 2
```

## Names inside dfns

Inside a dfn, plain assignment makes a local name. Modified and selective assignment update the nearest existing binding, which can be outside the dfn. An array has value semantics: changing one name leaves other copies unchanged.

```bpl
s←0 ⋄ f←{s←⍵ ⋄ s} ⋄ _←f 5 ⋄ s   ⍝ 0
s←0 ⋄ g←{s+←⍵ ⋄ s} ⋄ _←g 5 ⋄ s  ⍝ 5
a←1 2 ⋄ b←a ⋄ a₀←9 ⋄ b          ⍝ 1 2
```
